client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on me all day, and I can't seem to shake it no matter what I do. But honestly, what's weighing on me even more is watching my mom fall apart, and I have no idea how to be there for her without making things worse.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — carrying grief while also watching someone you love suffer is an incredibly heavy burden, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling weighed down. It sounds like part of you is holding back out of fear of saying or doing the "wrong" thing for your mom, which speaks to how deeply you care for her. I'm curious — when you imagine reaching out to her and it "going wrong," what does that moment look like in your mind?

client: When I imagine reaching out to my mom and it going wrong, I picture myself saying something clumsy about grandma, and then my mom just... shutting down or getting upset with me. And then instead of helping her, I've made things worse, and she's dealing with her grief AND my mess-up at the same time. It's like I'm so afraid of adding to her pain that I end up doing nothing, which I know probably isn't great either.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — you're caught between two painful options, where both acting and not acting feel like they could hurt her, so you freeze. It's worth gently noticing, though, that the "clumsy" thing you might say would come from a place of love, and your mom likely knows that about you even in her hardest moments. What do you think your mom actually needs from you right now — not the perfect version of support, but just *you* showing up in some small way?

client: I think what she probably needs is just to know I'm thinking about her, but even saying that out loud makes me feel guilty, like I've already been failing at that. I keep telling myself I'll call when I have the right words, and then days go by and I haven't called at all, which I'm sure makes it worse. I guess part of me is scared that if I show up as just "me," without anything helpful to offer, she'll feel more alone than if I hadn't reached out at all.
therapist: You just identified something really important — the belief that "just you" isn't enough, that your presence without perfect words has no value, and it's worth asking whether that's actually true or whether grief has convinced you of something that isn't quite fair to yourself. The very fact that you're losing sleep over how to support her *is* you showing up for her, even if she can't see it yet. What do you think she would say if you called her right now and simply said, "Mom, I've been thinking about you and I didn't know what to say, but I didn't want another day to go by without hearing your voice"?

client: I think she'd probably cry, and honestly that scares me more than the silence does. Like, if she cries, I don't know how to handle that either, and then I've just made things worse instead of better. It's like no matter what I do, I'm already imagining failing at it before I even try.
therapist: You just named something really powerful — that you're not actually afraid of *her* crying, but of not knowing what to do with her tears, which feels like a failure on your part. But here's a gentle reframe: her crying might not mean you've made things worse — it might mean she finally feels safe enough with you to let it out. What if her tears weren't a sign that you'd broken something, but that you'd actually reached her?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it's hard not to immediately think, "okay, but what do I actually do in that moment when she starts crying?" Like, even if her tears mean she feels safe, I'm still just standing there frozen, not knowing whether to hug her or say something or just stay quiet. It almost makes it feel more pressure-filled, not less, because now I'd be thinking "don't mess this up, this is actually a good thing happening."
therapist: That inner voice saying "don't mess this up" in the middle of a tender moment is such a heavy thing to carry, and it makes sense that even good moments start to feel like tests you could fail. The truth is, there's no wrong answer between a hug, words, or silence — your mom isn't grading you, she's just hoping to not feel alone. What do you think *you* would need from someone you love if the roles were reversed and you were the one crying?

client: I mean... if I were the one crying, I'd probably just want someone to be there, not say the perfect thing or fix anything. But that's kind of the problem, right? When I imagine being on the receiving end it feels simple, but when I'm actually standing in front of my mom I just freeze and that voice kicks in and suddenly I'm calculating every move instead of just being present.
therapist: You just gave yourself the most honest and compassionate answer — that presence matters more than perfection — and some part of you already knows this is true, even if that critical voice drowns it out in the moment. It sounds like the real challenge isn't knowing *what* to do, but learning to quiet that calculating voice long enough to let yourself just *be* with her. I wonder, what do you think that voice is ultimately trying to protect you from?

client: That's... actually a question I haven't thought about before. I think maybe it's trying to protect me from being a disappointment — like if I calculate everything perfectly, I can't be blamed for failing her. But the irony is that all that calculating is probably exactly what's making me feel so distant from her in the first place.
therapist: That insight is genuinely profound — you've just traced the whole loop: the fear of disappointing her is creating the very distance that's making you feel like you're already failing her. That protective voice meant well, but it's been working against the connection you both clearly need right now. What would it feel like to make one small, imperfect move toward her this week — not a perfect call, just a real one?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it — like, intellectually I can see the loop you're describing. But the idea of making that call, even a small one, makes my chest tighten up immediately, because what if I say the wrong thing and it just confirms to her that I'm not really there for her the way she needs? It feels less like a small step and more like walking up to the edge of something I can't take back.
therapist: That tightening in your chest is real and worth honoring — it's telling you that this matters deeply to you, and that's not a weakness, it's love. But I want to gently reflect something back: you've been so focused on the fear of one wrong word confirming you're not there for her, yet a month of silence hasn't confirmed that to you yet — which suggests she may be holding more grace for you than you're allowing yourself to believe. What do you think it would mean about *you* as a person if she did feel hurt by an imperfect call — would that truly make you someone who isn't there for her, or just someone who is also grieving and trying their best?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Because when I really sit with it... I guess one imperfect call wouldn't make me a bad friend, but there's this voice in my head that says the silence itself already proves I'm failing her. And I think what scares me is that if I reach out now and she does seem hurt or distant, I won't be able to handle that confirmation on top of everything else I'm already carrying with my own grief.
therapist: You're carrying so much right now — your own grief for your grandmother, the fear of losing closeness with your mom, and the weight of a story you've been telling yourself that the silence already means something damning about you. It's worth noticing that you haven't actually *received* confirmation that she's hurt or distant — you've been living inside a painful verdict that hasn't been handed down yet. I'm wondering, what are you afraid you'd find out about your own ability to cope if you reached out and things felt hard — do you trust yourself at all to survive a difficult moment with her?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think part of me is afraid that if I reach out and she does seem distant or hurt, I'll just fall apart completely — like I won't be able to hold myself together while I'm already grieving my grandmother. And I guess I don't really trust myself that much right now, because I've been feeling so fragile that even small things have been setting me off.
therapist: That fragility you're describing makes complete sense — you're grieving, you're scared, and you've been holding a lot alone for a month, so of course your trust in yourself feels shaky right now. But I want to gently point out that you've actually been surviving this fragility every single day, even when it's felt unbearable — which means some part of you is more resilient than that frightened voice is giving you credit for. When you imagine "falling apart" after a hard call with your mom, what does that actually look like to you — and is falling apart necessarily the same thing as not being able to get back up?
